extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors of systematic reviews, health technology assessment authors, meta-analysts, and evidence-synthesis methodologists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence for identifying, preventing, detecting and minimising publication and related (dissemination) biases in systematic reviews and meta-analyses of health-care research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for inclusion in the HTA journal series
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports are published in the HTA journal series if (1) they have resulted from work for the HTA programme, and (2) they are of a sufficiently high scientific quality as assessed by the referees and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final reports are peer reviewed by independent expert referees before publication; HTA editors attempt to ensure accuracy but do not accept liability for material published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'systematic' review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews in Health Technology Assessment are termed ‘systematic’ when the account of the search, appraisal and synthesis methods (to minimise biases and random errors) would, in theory, permit the replication of the review by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, replicable description of search, appraisal and synthesis methods is required; transparency of methods is a core quality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify included studies as evidence or method studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence studies provide empirical evidence on the existence, consequences, causes and/or risk factors of dissemination bias; method studies develop or evaluate methods for preventing, reducing or detecting dissemination bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification when selecting and extracting data to appropriately synthesise different kinds of contributions (empirical findings vs methodological development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive literature searching across multiple databases and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Search multiple electronic databases (e.g. Cochrane Methodology Register Database, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, OpenSIGLE) and examine reference lists of retrieved studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad database search plus reference checking increases capture of relevant evidence about dissemination bias and methods; searches may be updated to capture recent studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dual checking in review conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The identified studies were classified by one reviewer as evidence or method studies and checked by a second reviewer; one reviewer extracted data directly into tables which were checked by a second reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ at least two reviewers (classification and extraction with checking) to reduce errors and bias in the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction and synthesis principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Data extraction into specifically designed tables according to types of bias or methods; evidence from empirical studies summarised narratively and, where appropriate, results quantitatively pooled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tailored extraction forms, narrative synthesis for heterogeneous evidence, and quantitative pooling/meta-analysis when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and apply methods by stage of the review (prevent/detect/minimise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Available methods can be classified according to the stage of a literature review: to prevent publication bias before a literature review, to detect it during a literature review, or to minimise its impact after a literature review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prevent = prospective registration of trials; detect = locating unpublished studies, funnel plot and related tests, sensitivity analysis modelling; minimise = confirmatory large-scale trials, updating the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective registration of trials (prevention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective registration of clinical trials at inception is an important solution to publication bias; the ICMJE compulsory policy (2004) and WHO standards are influential initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration alone is insufficient — results of registered trials must be publicly accessible; systematic reviewers should search trial registers and contact trialists for results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make results of registered trials publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of prospective trial registration itself is not sufficient; it is important to make sure that results of registered trials are publicly accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial registers are useful only if reviewers search them, use the data they provide and contact trialists where studies have not yet been published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search trial registries and locate ongoing or unpublished trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clinical trial registries and electronic publication of trial results to identify ongoing or unpublished clinical trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching registries and contacting investigators can help detect unpublished data and reduce the risk of dissemination bias in reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically search for grey literature and unpublished studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate and include grey literature or unpublished studies as part of literature searching to reduce bias from published-only evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grey literature may be small or lower quality but can differ systematically from published studies; inclusion should be systematic and explicitly reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-English-language studies where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Including non-English-language studies can reduce bias; exclusion of non-English language studies appears to result in a particularly high risk of bias in some research areas (e.g. complementary and alternative medicine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviewers should consider searching for and including non-English studies and report language restrictions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the risk of publication bias using multiple approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the risk of publication bias includes locating unpublished studies, funnel plot and related statistical tests, sensitivity analysis modelling, and other statistical or modelling methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of methods (searching, statistical tests, modelling and qualitative judgement) rather than relying on a single approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use funnel plot and related statistical tests cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Funnel plot and related statistical tests have been widely used to assess publication bias, but the interpretation of their results was often too simplistic and likely misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret funnel plots cautiously (they are indirect and exploratory); use them mainly as part of sensitivity analyses and consider alternative explanations for asymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply statistical and modelling methods appropriately (sensitivity analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: All statistical methods, simple or complex, are indirect and exploratory and are often based on assumptions that can be difficult to justify; the available statistical methods can be useful for the purpose of sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical methods to explore robustness of results, not as definitive proof of bias; report assumptions and limitations clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sophisticated modelling methods where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: More sophisticated modelling methods exist but have not been widely used, possibly because of complexity and lack of user-friendly software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible and justified, consider advanced modelling approaches to estimate and adjust for dissemination bias, and report modelling choices and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of fixed or random-effects models
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of fixed or random-effects models is relevant when synthesising results and when investigating bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select model type based on heterogeneity and review objectives; report rationale for choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating systematic reviews to minimise impact of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Updating systematic reviews can help minimise the impact of publication bias after a literature review (e.g. by incorporating newly published confirmatory large-scale trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for and report strategies for updating reviews; updates can change pooled estimates when new data become available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and endorse reporting guidelines to reduce reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The prospective registration of clinical trials and the endorsement of reporting guidelines (e.g. CONSORT) may reduce research dissemination bias in clinical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals, funders and researchers should endorse and adhere to reporting guidelines to improve completeness and transparency of published reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly report methods used to detect/prevent dissemination bias in published reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In surveys, assessors judged whether systematic reviews located and included non-English-language studies, grey literature/unpublished studies, and tested for publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviews should explicitly state what methods were used to reduce/detect publication bias (databases searched, grey literature, language restrictions, statistical tests, registry searches, contact of authors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop qualitative methods to assess risk of publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Further research is needed to develop methods for qualitatively assessing the risk of publication bias in systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until standard qualitative assessment methods exist, reviewers should transparently document potential sources of dissemination bias and their judgement about likely direction and magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey and quality-assessment sampling procedures for reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When surveying published systematic reviews, randomly select reviews from databases (e.g. MEDLINE) stratified by review type (treatment, diagnostic accuracy, association, gene–disease) and assess methods used to deal with publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random sampling and predefined strata to assess the prevalence of methods addressing dissemination bias across review types; report sampling and assessment procedures.
